items.item: A run pointing at a recipe version rather than a recipe is the same idea as topic 1's SCD rows: the thing that changes over time needs a stable reference to the exact version in force, not to a name that silently drifts underneath it.

items.item: ISA-88's physical model and ISA-95's equipment hierarchy both nest physical plant structure, but they are different standards built for different purposes (batch control procedure vs. enterprise/control data ownership) and neither publicly states a level-for-level mapping between them.

at.step: Reveal: two standards, two models, named separately

items.item: A rework loop is not a modelling mistake to be designed away — real production genuinely reworks rejected material — which is exactly why the query layer, not the schema, has to be the thing that guarantees termination.

at.step: Predict: does an unprotected loop in the data ever stop a recursive query on its own?

items.item: Filling an artificial depth cap rather than stopping short of it is the only way to demonstrate non-termination in a bounded test; the executed run here hits exactly the row count the cap allows, every single time, which is itself the evidence.

at.step: Reveal: run it for real, capped, and watch it never stop short of the cap

items.item: A reachability query is only as complete as its edge table — there is no way for the query itself to know an edge is missing, because a missing edge looks identical to a true absence of a relationship.

at.step: Reveal: one missing edge, and the exact lots a recall would miss

items.item: A query over an edge table scales linearly in this sandbox's small example, but the syllabus's own pointer to a dedicated graph database (§17.4, skipped in this course) exists precisely because a recursive CTE's per-step join cost stops being free once the graph and the recall depth both grow large.

Every later topic in this chapter that references 'the lot' or 'the run' (quality, OEE) treats these entities as already-modelled facts; this topic is where their actual table shapes and join keys get decided.

Backward genealogy (finding every raw-material ancestor) and forward genealogy (finding every downstream exposure) are the same recursive mechanism run in opposite directions over the same edge table, not two different algorithms.

at.step: Reveal: the real recall list, traced forward from one contaminated lot

items.item: A lot's consume/produce edges are naturally a DAG for straight-through production, but a real rework loop (reject material folded back into an earlier stage) breaks that assumption in practice, which is exactly why the course treats the graph as DAG-shaped with one named exception rather than purely acyclic.

at.step: Predict: does an unprotected loop in the data ever stop a recursive query on its own?

items.item: ISA-88's own standard is explicit that a run's recipe reference is to a specific recipe version with its own formula and procedure, which is the production-floor reason a work order can't simply point at a product name and expect reproducibility.
